entries.name: Partial Information Decomposition
entries.senseHere: A method for splitting the total information that two or more source neurons carry about a target neuron into separate pieces: information shared redundantly by the sources, information unique to each source, and information that only emerges from their joint pattern (synergy).
entries.background: Introduced by Williams and Beer as a way to go beyond ordinary mutual information, which only measures how much two variables share without distinguishing these different modes of information sharing.

entries.name: rich club
entries.senseHere: The subset of best-connected neurons in a network that are more densely interconnected with each other than chance would predict; shown to concentrate most of the network's synergistic computation despite containing a minority of neurons.

entries.name: multielectrode array
entries.senseHere: A grid of many recording electrodes placed against neural tissue, able to detect spiking activity from hundreds of individual neurons simultaneously, forming the raw data later converted into effective networks and analyzed with PID.

entries.name: mutual information
entries.senseHere: A number measuring how much knowing the state of one neuron reduces uncertainty about the state of another, used here as a baseline quantity that PID then breaks apart into redundant, unique and synergistic pieces.

entries.name: transfer entropy
entries.senseHere: A directional measure of how much a neuron's past activity reduces uncertainty about another neuron's future activity, beyond what that second neuron's own past already tells us; used to build networks of information flow between neurons and identify the 'computational triads' later fed into PID.

entries.name: effective connectivity
entries.senseHere: A description of directed influence between neurons, i.e. how one neuron's past activity shapes another's future, as measured by transfer entropy; contrasted in the article with the undirected, purely statistical association captured by functional connectivity (mutual information).

entries.name: synergy
entries.senseHere: The portion of information about a target neuron's activity that can only be learned by observing two (or more) source neurons' joint pattern together, not from either source alone; treated throughout the article as the signature of genuine neural computation or 'information processing'.

entries.name: redundancy
entries.senseHere: The information about a target neuron that could be learned equally well from either source neuron alone, so that adding the second source tells you nothing new.

entries.name: unique information
entries.senseHere: The information about a target neuron's activity that only one particular source neuron can supply, not obtainable from the other source.

entries.name: redundancy function
entries.senseHere: A formally chosen rule for measuring exactly how much information counts as redundant between sources; since no single agreed rule exists, different choices of this function give different PID results, and much of the practical difficulty in applying PID is choosing one suited to the data.

entries.name: Imin
entries.senseHere: The original, most widely used redundancy function proposed alongside PID itself, defined for discrete data; criticized elsewhere for giving unintuitive results in some cases but still the measure behind most of the empirical neural findings discussed.

entries.name: computational triad
entries.senseHere: The basic unit analyzed throughout the empirical sections: two source neurons that both send significant transfer-entropy connections to one common target neuron, on which a full PID can be performed.

entries.name: partial information lattice
entries.senseHere: A structured diagram ordering every possible combination of source neurons by which combinations' information is a subset of which others, used to systematically calculate every distinct redundant, unique, or synergistic piece of information in a multi-source system.

entries.name: organotypic cultures
entries.senseHere: Living slices of mouse cortex grown in a dish that retain much of the original tissue's natural connectivity pattern, used as the experimental system for most of the PID-based findings described.

entries.name: O-information
entries.senseHere: A simpler, more scalable summary measure that approximates whether a group of variables is, on balance, more redundant or more synergistic overall, trading the full detail of PID for the ability to handle larger groups of neurons.

entries.name: Dedekind number
entries.senseHere: A rapidly growing count (from a branch of combinatorics) that gives the number of distinct information pieces in a full PID lattice for a given number of source neurons; used to explain why full PID becomes computationally intractable once there are more than a handful of sources.

entries.name: local PID
entries.senseHere: A version of PID applied to single specific moments or configurations of neural activity rather than averaged over all possible states, producing a time-resolved trace of redundancy, uniqueness and synergy rather than one overall expected value.

entries.name: Integrated Information Decomposition
entries.senseHere: An extension of PID that decomposes information shared between groups of variables across time or across multiple target variables at once, rather than just one target, enabling study of how redundancy and synergy evolve dynamically or connect multiple brain measures.

entries.name: Möbius inversion
entries.senseHere: A mathematical procedure applied to the partial information lattice that calculates the value of each individual information piece by subtracting out everything already accounted for by simpler combinations lower on the lattice.
